content.question_text: What is the difference between 'call by value' and 'call by reference' in programming languages?

core_requirements: Call by value means the method gets a copy of the value that the caller provides — it cannot modify the original variable.
Call by reference means the method gets the location of the variable that the caller provides — it can modify the value stored there.
acceptable_variations: Call by value = copy of value; call by reference = access to the original variable's memory location.

content.question_text: Does Java use call by value or call by reference? What does this mean in practice?

core_requirements: Java always uses call by value.
This means the method gets a copy of all arguments and cannot modify the contents of any variable in the method call.
acceptable_variations: Java is always call by value — methods work on copies, never originals.

content.question_text: What are the two kinds of method parameters in Java?
Can a method modify a primitive type parameter? Explain with the tripleValue example.

core_requirements: No — a method cannot modify a primitive type parameter.
When tripleValue(percent) is called, x gets a copy of percent's value (10). x is tripled to 30, but percent remains 10. When the method ends, x is discarded and percent is unchanged.
acceptable_variations: Primitive parameters are copies — changes inside the method have no effect on the original variable.

content.question_text: Can a method change the state of an object parameter? Explain why.

core_requirements: Yes — a method can change the state of an object parameter.
The method receives a copy of the object reference, but both the copy and the original refer to the same object. Calling mutator methods through the copied reference modifies the actual object.
acceptable_variations: Object reference is copied, but both copies point to the same object — so state changes are visible outside the method.

content.question_text: Can a method make an object parameter refer to a new object? Explain why not, using the swap example.

core_requirements: No — a method cannot make an object parameter refer to a new object.

In the swap(Employee x, Employee y) example, x and y are copies of the references a and b. The method swaps the copies, but when it ends the parameter variables are discarded. The original variables a and b still refer to the same objects as before the call.
acceptable_variations: The method swaps copies of references — the originals are unaffected. Java does not use call by reference for objects.

content.question_text: Summarize the three things a method can and cannot do with method parameters in Java.

core_requirements: A method cannot modify a parameter of a primitive type (number types, char, or boolean).
A method can change the state of an object parameter.
A method cannot make an object parameter refer to a new object.
acceptable_variations: Cannot change primitives; can mutate object state; cannot reassign object references.
